rationale: The two abstracts differ only in whether the memory-responsive patches lie posterior (Option 1) or anterior (Option 2) to the scene perception areas. The paper proposes a convergence zone at the posterior edge of high-level visual cortex, interfacing sensory and mnemonic representations while avoiding interference. A posterior location fits the proposed account of adjacent yet distinct sensory and memory regions, so Option 1 supports the paper's hypothesis more directly.

The paper proposes that the Pdyn+ CeA-to-PBN pathway regulates itch. Option 1 reports that stimulating this pathway increases scratching, enhances PBN Fos, and lowers pain thresholds, which supports a pro-itch, pro-nociceptive role for the pathway as hypothesized. Option 2 reports the opposite: stimulation inhibits scratching, suppresses PBN Fos, and raises thresholds. Option 2 would argue against the pathway promoting itch, so Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper's proposed account is that endothelial cells show regional homogeneity and that AD endothelial cells have downregulated protein folding genes, with similar responses to plaques and CAA. Option 1 matches this account (homogeneity, downregulated protein folding). Option 2 reports heterogeneity and upregulated protein folding, which contradicts the paper's central framing. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that hippocampal theta is a key modulator of memory, consistent with computational models, and that narrowband theta masked by broadband effects is the relevant signal. Option 2 reports theta increases during encoding and recall, directly supporting the theta-memory account the paper defends. Option 1 reports theta decreases, which contradicts the stated models and the paper's own framing of theta as memory-relevant. Thus Option 2 is clearly better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that motion cues alone can drive robust object category responses. Option 1 reports posterior occipitotemporal and ventral regions decoding better for dynamic stimuli and anterior/dorsal for static, which fits a motion-as-category-cue account in ventral cortex (the paper's emphasis on dynamic luminance cues matching). Option 2 reverses the regional pattern, placing the dynamic advantage in anterior/dorsal regions, which is less consistent with the narrative that motion supports ventral category processing. Option 1 is modestly better news for the proposed account.

Both abstracts are identical except for which sex shows the PrL-DT relationship and drug-seeking link. Option 1 attributes the proposed PrL mechanism and its link to drug-seeking to males; Option 2 attributes it to females. The paper's proposed account is that PrL activity underlies distress tolerance and predicts drug-seeking. Option 1 supports this account in the sex the paper emphasizes, while Option 2 does too but for females. Since the hypothesis itself (PrL role in DT and drug-seeking) is supported equally in both, the difference is mainly which sex is highlighted, so the news value is near neutral, with a slight edge to Option 1 for the sexes' distinct effects being framed as a clean male finding.

The two abstracts are identical except for which brain region is linked to mean control versus covariance control. The paper proposes a stochastic control framework that decomposes control cost into mean and covariance components. Option 1 reports lower visual areas controlling means and PCC controlling covariances; Option 2 reverses this. Neither result clearly favors the framework itself, since the framework's utility is shown either way. The difference is only which region is assigned to which component, so it is roughly neutral for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that age-related differences in fluid intelligence are partly mediated by frontoparietal responsiveness to cognitive demand. Option 1 says mediation is specifically associated with voxels most activated by cognitive demand, which directly supports the proposed frontoparietal activation account. Option 2 says mediation is associated with voxels suppressed by demand and not activated ones, which undercuts the activation-based mechanism the paper defends. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis. The physical-activity moderation details are exploratory and secondary.

The paper proposes that danger shifts consolidation from PRh toward BLA, with initial pairings encoded in BLA and later pairings in PRh, plus mutual inhibition between regions. Option 1 matches this account exactly. Option 2 reverses the regional assignments (BLA to PRh shift, PRh encoding initial pairings), contradicting the proposed model. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's hypothesis better.

Both abstracts describe the same design and the same lateral-to-medial partition development, but Option 1 reports faster lateral thalamus development, linear increases in fiber integrity, and frontal connections developing later, while Option 2 reports reduction, decrease, earlier frontal development, and slower lateral development. The paper's proposed account is a posterior-to-anterior developmental gradient of thalamocortical connectivity. Option 1's frontal-later finding is consistent with a posterior-to-anterior gradient, whereas Option 2's frontal-earlier finding contradicts it. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's account better.

The paper argues that cortico-thalamic feedback drives state-dependent modulation of dLGN visual responses. Option 2 supports this claim (silencing feedback reduces state differences, for both temporal and spatial features), whereas Option 1 reports that silencing feedback increases state differences, which would undercut the feedback-dependence account. Option 2 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

Both options share the same framework: ON/OFF pathway dominance shifting with contrast. The paper's proposed account is that high-contrast stimuli favor OFF dominance and low-contrast favor ON dominance, with ON pathways more contrast-sensitive. Option 1 matches this account exactly, including the predicted loss of low-contrast vision with ON deficits, so it supports the paper's hypothesis more strongly than Option 2, which reverses the contrast-polarity relationship and conflicts with the stated higher ON contrast sensitivity.

The two abstracts differ only in the topography and band pairings: Option 1 links saccade rhythms to occipital theta and fixation rhythms to whole-head delta; Option 2 swaps these to whole-head theta and occipital delta. The paper's proposed account is that linguistic processing imposes endogenous rhythms on reading. Option 1's pairing of word-level saccades with occipital (visual) activity and sentence-level fixation rhythms with whole-head activity fits more naturally with a visual-sampling and higher-level chunking story, though the difference is modest and both preserve the core claim.

The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 reports the abstraction benefit and neural responses for SWS cueing, while Option 2 reports them for REM cueing. The paper proposes that targeted memory reactivation during sleep facilitates visual rule abstraction, with SWS as the favored stage given the framing of SWS-linked plasticity. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's central account more directly, making it better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that VTA dopamine neurons provide motivational value to actions and cues (critic-like role, flexible persistent pursuit) while SNc neurons support precise, action-specific learning (actor-like role). Option 1 assigns these functions as the paper's framework states. Option 2 swaps VTA and SNc roles, which contradicts the proposed separable-systems architecture and the stated actor-critic mapping. Thus Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in the signs of the pupil-neural/vascular correlations and the blink effect. Option 1 reports positive correlations during rest and NREM and blinking associated with decreased arousal and increased blood volume during sleep, consistent with the paper's framing that arousal drives coupled neural and vascular dynamics (pupil tracks gamma and blood volume). Option 2 reverses these signs, which would undercut the claimed coupling pattern and the blink-related arousal account. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed account better.

The paper proposes that tonotopic organization extends to the cochlear apex in low-frequency animals, consistent with the base-of-cochlea pattern established by von Békésy and later work. Option 2 reports responses differing across the apex in a pattern consistent with the base, supporting the paper's account of an orderly tonotopic map. Option 1 reports no such difference, which would undermine the proposed tonotopic account. Option 2 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's position.

Both abstracts share the same core claim: respiration dynamically entrains prefrontal activity depending on behavioral state. The only difference is which state shows stronger gamma entrainment (HC in Option 1, TS in Option 2) and which shows superficial-layer recruitment. Option 1 has gamma entrainment strongest in home cage, which is the baseline/resting state and a plausible, unsurprising finding for a respiration-coupling account; Option 2 frames tail-suspension stress as the state of strongest gamma entrainment, a more striking stress-linked result that could support a state-dependent stress-engagement narrative. Neither clearly strengthens the paper's central claim more than the other, so the difference is roughly neutral, with a slight tilt toward Option 2 for a more interesting state-dependent framing.

The paper proposes that otitis media-related auditory deprivation alters the descending olivocochlear efferent system, impairing speech-in-noise recognition. Option 1 reports stronger efferent inhibition and lower SNR thresholds (better performance) in the otitis media group; Option 2 reports weaker inhibition and higher SNR needed (worse performance). Option 2 aligns with the paper's hypothesis of impaired central auditory processing linked to efferent changes, so Option 1 is worse news for the proposed account.

The paper proposes that hV6A sends signals to M1 via a short parieto-frontal route during reach planning. Option 1 reports inhibition of MEPs by hV6A, Option 2 reports facilitation. For a hypothesis that the parieto-frontal pathway actively contributes to reach planning, a clear, interpretable directional effect (facilitation, consistent with excitatory drive toward motor output) is typically read as more supportive of an active functional connection than inhibition, which is harder to link to a planning role. Both options support the core claim of an active short route, so the difference is moderately favorable to Option 2.

The paper proposes that corticofugal signals engage intracollicular excitatory circuits via recurrent inhibition of GABA neurons, dampening corticofugal activity and driving glutamatergic IC neurons. Option 1 matches this mechanism: tonically firing glutamatergic neurons are excited, GABA neurons fire during repetitive activity, and polysynaptic inhibition of glutamatergic neurons generates local excitation. Option 2 reverses the cell types, making glutamatergic neurons the GABA-driven targets and yielding local inhibition, which contradicts the paper's proposed account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes an internal model for vibrissa positioning. Option 1 finds peripheral reafference is not required and motor cortex is needed only without reafference, supporting a flexible internal model that works through either mechanism. Option 2 finds both reafference and motor cortex are required, which implies a model that depends on external feedback and cortex together. The internal-model account the paper defends is more sharply supported by Option 1's dissociable, redundant mechanisms, since it explains the results without requiring every component; Option 2 is a more restrictive, less parsimonious conclusion that the paper's framing ('requires either') would not match.

The paper proposes that a global rise of inhibition (from FSNs) drives initiation and execution of spontaneous motor actions. Option 1 supports this directly: FSNs fire longer and earlier, carry more movement-onset information, show stereotyped responses, and silencing FSNs reduces licking. Option 2 reverses these findings, attributing the drive to excitation from PNs, which contradicts the paper's proposed account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in swapping which measure (CT or SA) shows the anterior-posterior division versus the within-lobe pattern, and which measure shows the strongest neonate-adult similarity in the medial surface. The paper's proposed account is that CT and SA have distinct genetic topographies established in the neonatal brain. Option 1 matches the prior adult literature's pattern that SA is more anterior-posterior organized and CT more lobe-organized, and places the medial CT similarity, which is consistent with the paper's framing of differential genetic regulation. Option 2 reverses these assignments, which is less coherent with the stated hypothesis of differential CT/SA genetic patterning, so Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ only in which neuron type shows greater Ca2+ influx and compact active zone organization: Option 1 assigns these to tonic release sites, Option 2 to phasic. The paper's proposed account is that nano-architecture and Ca2+ influx together tune release differently across tonic and phasic subtypes; both versions support that account equally. The directional difference is a matter of which subtype is favored, not a clear gain or loss for the central hypothesis, so the news value for the paper's proposed account is roughly neutral, with Option 1 marginally aligning with the expected pattern of tonic synapses having more compact, Ca-channel-enriched sites.

The two abstracts are identical except Option 1 places Sema5A/5B expression in the pons at the decussation site, while Option 2 places it in the medulla. The paper's proposed account is that Sema5A/5B-PlexA1/A3 signaling inhibits premature defasciculation of CS axons at the decussation site. Anatomically, the pyramidal decussation occurs in the caudal medulla, so Option 2's medullary localization is more consistent with the claimed mechanism, making Option 2 marginally better support for the paper's account. The difference is small and mainly about anatomical precision.

Both abstracts propose the same hypothesis: NMJ cleft alkalization driven by postsynaptic Ca2+ and PMCA, with acidification under strenuous stimulation. The key difference is Option 1 reports a 'significant reduction of alkalization' at 5 s stimulation, while Option 2 reports a 'significant and prolonged alkalization.' Option 2's result more directly supports the paper's proposed mechanism of activity-induced alkalization via muscle Ca2+ extrusion, so Option 1 is worse news for the paper's account.

The paper's hypothesis is that activity-dependent glutamate receptor signaling mediates visual map alignment in the SC. Option 1 reports AMPA receptor knockout disrupting L5-V1 terminal organization with retinocollicular topography unaffected, supporting a role for AMPA receptors. Option 2 reports the same pattern for NMDA receptors. Both are equally supportive of the paper's central account (receptor-mediated activity-dependent alignment), so the choice between them is roughly neutral for the proposed mechanism, with the study's framing of AMPA receptors as the mediator in Option 1 being comparable to NMDA in Option 2.

The two abstracts differ only in whether MFN2 was overexpressed (Option 1) or knocked down (Option 2). Both report the same qualitative outcomes: reduced trafficking and fusion, decreased SV proteins, inhibited exocytosis, Ca2+ dyshomeostasis, and enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ sequestration. The paper's proposed account is an active fusion-related QC process supporting presynaptic Ca2+ handling and the SV cycle. Since the reported effects are the same in direction under either manipulation, the choice of overexpression versus knockdown does not clearly favor the paper's hypothesis either way.

The paper proposes that α9k1 integrin signaling drives CNS sensory regeneration via a distinctive program. Option 1 reports the CNS program shows little correlation with embryonic or PNS programs, supporting the claim that it is distinctive and not a recapitulation of developmental or PNS regeneration. Option 2 reports high correlation, undermining the 'distinctive program' claim. Thus Option 1 is better news for the paper's account.

The paper proposes that hallucination proneness reflects indirect alterations in perceptual priors dependent on sensory noise. Option 1 reports a general prior bias related to sensory noise and sensory resolution, supporting the indirect, noise-dependent account. Option 2 reports a circumscribed bias unrelated to sensory noise, supporting a direct prior-alteration account, which contradicts the paper's proposed mechanism. Thus Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's defended hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in wording: Option 1 says assemblies 'disintegrate' into smaller complexes or 'segregation domains' with intercellular structures shared, while Option 2 says intracellular structures are shared and 'entangle' them into 'larger complexes' or 'association domains'. The paper's proposed account is that transsynaptic assemblies physically link the three compartments and organize into functional domains resembling nanocolumns. Option 2's larger, entangled complexes and association domains fit that connected-organization account better than Option 1's disintegration into smaller segregated units, so Option 1 is somewhat worse news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that GluA1 ubiquitination at K868 is needed for proper bidirectional plasticity and cognition. Option 1 reports enhanced LTP with LTD deficits; Option 2 reports the reverse. Both report cognitive deficits. The proposed account is that ubiquitination regulates AMPAR stability and thus bidirectional plasticity; blocking it (K868R) should disrupt that balance in either direction, so the direction of the LTP/LTD change is not clearly favoring one. Option 1's LTP enhancement with LTD deficit is a somewhat less intuitive reading of loss of degradation-driven AMPAR turnover, but both are consistent with a disrupted bidirectional system, making the difference modest.

Both abstracts report the same core findings: patient-derived aqueous extracts inhibit LTP, tau is required with Abeta, and effects persist. The paper's proposed hypothesis is that diffusible tau drives synaptic dysfunction. Option 1 says tau heightens the threshold for Abeta (tau is protective or dampening), and describes a slow onset of tau-driven deficits. Option 2 says tau lowers the threshold for Abeta (tau sensitizes, consistent with promoting Abeta toxicity), and describes rapid onset. Option 2 aligns better with the paper's conclusion that diffusible tau promotes Abeta-mediated dysfunction and causes rapid onset deficits, so Option 1 is worse news for the proposed hypothesis.

Both abstracts propose the same hypothesis: ELS-activated neuronal ensembles are reactivated by adult stress and encode stress hypersensitivity. Option 1 reports that inhibiting ELS-activated NAc neurons ameliorates social avoidance, which supports the proposed account that these ensembles drive stress hypersensitivity. Option 2 reports the opposite direction in CA1 (exacerbated avoidance) and uses hM3Dq, a mismatch with inhibition. That result is inconsistent with the paper's proposed mechanism, so Option 1 is clearly better news for the hypothesis.

The paper argues that the ongoing local inhibitory barrage produces the irregular firing of GPe neurons in vivo. Option 1 shows silencing PV+ neurons decreases PV- firing rate and regularity, and dynamic clamp with inhibition reduces irregularity, supporting the barrage-as-source-of-irregularity account. Option 2 reverses these: silencing increases irregularity and inhibition increases irregularity, which contradicts the paper's proposed account that the barrage generates the irregular pattern. Option 1 therefore is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

Both abstracts describe the same proposed account: PVT as a stress sensor tuning dmPFC inhibitory circuits to modulate probabilistic fear memory. Option 1 reports repetitive stress activating PVT, GABA-neuron mediated suppression of PV cells, enhanced synaptic modification during conditioning that helps form the memory, and disruption of the original memory. Option 2 reports acute stress, somatostatin neurons, impaired synaptic modification that abolishes memory formation, and preservation of the memory. The paper's proposed account is that PVT-driven circuit modulation shapes memory; Option 1's findings (memory formation facilitated, memory disrupted by modulation) align more directly with a strong, mechanistic role for the stress-PVT-dmPFC pathway in altering memory, whereas Option 2's findings suggest the pathway merely preserves memory and abolishes formation, which is a somewhat weaker and less coherent demonstration of the proposed sensor role.

The paper proposes that GC GLP-1R+ neurons suppress food intake (homeostatic and hedonic) via GLP-1R agonism. Option 1 reports depolarization by exendin-4, chemogenetic stimulation reducing intake, and GC GLP-1R agonism reducing intake, all consistent with the proposed satiety role. Option 2 reports polarization (ambiguous/likely hyperpolarization, a mismatch with depolarization), and stimulation increasing intake, which contradicts the proposed account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper argues that pupil size and alpha power are multifaceted, modality-dependent indices of cognitive demand, not interchangeable measures. Option 1 reports pupil size increasing with difficulty (a standard effort marker) and alpha decreasing with visual difficulty (the classic alpha-desynchronization-with-load pattern), plus a negative pupil-alpha trial correlation. Option 2 reverses these: pupil decreasing with demand and alpha increasing, with a positive correlation. Option 2's pattern would undermine the conventional account of pupil dilation and alpha as demand/effort indices that the paper engages with, so Option 1 is better news for the paper's framing.

The paper proposes that VGLUT3 is a vital contributor to HD pathophysiology and a viable therapeutic target. The two versions differ in mechanism details: Option 1 reports activation of Akt/ERK1/2 and short-term memory rescue with no change in microgliosis; Option 2 reports suppression of Akt/ERK1/2, long-term memory rescue, and no change in astrogliosis. Activation of pro-survival Akt/ERK1/2 signaling fits a neuroprotective account of VGLUT3 deletion better than suppression, which would be a less coherent survival mechanism. Option 1's microgliosis readout is also a neuroinflammation measure, while Option 2's astrogliosis is a different cell type; neither clearly favors the proposed hypothesis. Overall Option 1 is modestly better news for the paper's neuroprotection account.

The paper proposes that inhibitory control deficits in heroin addiction, shown by impaired sensitivity and hyperactivation in cognitive control regions, contribute to self-control lapses. Option 1 reports hyperactivations and higher sensitivity, which frames the neurobehavioral deficit as compensatory hyperactivation rather than hypoactivation, departing from the hypoactivation account the introduction cites. Option 2 reports hypoactivation and lower sensitivity, matching the common PFC hypoactivation model of addiction and the paper's framing of deficits. Option 2 is the more coherent support for the paper's deficit-based account, so Option 1 is worse news for it.

The paper proposes that autism involves weakened predictive feedback 'priors' reducing global contour integration. Option 2 (attenuated illusory contour responses) fits this account directly, supporting the weakened-priors idea. Option 1 (enhanced responses) would contradict the proposed mechanism's implications, so it is worse news for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: the hippocampus is critical for temporal discounting when outcomes are experienced in the moment, not when hypothetical. The only difference is the direction of the lesion effect on the delay-reward trade-off amplitude. Option 1 reports decreased amplitude, meaning hippocampal lesions reduce sensitivity to delay, with persistent choice of delayed options. That reduced trade-off reflects the impaired discounting the paper argues for, supporting its account that the hippocampus drives experiential temporal discounting. Option 2 reports increased amplitude, which would mean stronger delay sensitivity after lesions, contradicting the claimed impairment pattern. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper argues that long-term mAChR activation uncovers a plastic subset of CA3 neurons whose hyperadaptation phenotype depends on the M-current. Option 1 says M-channel antagonists and AChR agonist reapplication enhance the hyperadaptation phenotype, which is consistent with an M-current-driven mechanism. Option 2 says these manipulations abolish it, which would also be consistent with M-current dependence but suggests a different direction of modulation. Option 1 fits the paper's framing that the phenotype is characterized by a strong M-current and modulated by cholinergic agents more directly, so it reads as somewhat better support for the proposed account.

The paper proposes a physiological role for presynaptic APP at medial perforant path synapses. Option 1 reports APP deficiency altering excitatory neurotransmission and presynaptic deletion increasing efficacy, which supports a role for APP as a modulator of excitatory transmission. Option 2 reports altered inhibitory neurotransmission and decreased efficacy, which would be a different and less coherent story relative to the excitatory-synapse framing of the study. Option 1 therefore fits the paper's proposed account somewhat better.

The paper's proposed account is that insula DYN/KOR microcircuitry drives excessive alcohol use. Option 1 reports that DYN deletion blocks escalation and reduces intake, KOR antagonism reduces early intake, and IA reduces excitability while increasing excitatory drive, all consistent with a mechanism promoting alcohol use being engaged and then targetable. Option 2 reports the opposite directions for each finding (DYN deletion increases intake, KOR antagonism increases intake, IA increases excitability and decreases excitatory drive), which would undercut a model where this circuit promotes excessive drinking. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that predictable natural sequences (NSeqs) of USVs are important and that they are encoded selectively in auditory cortex, with social experience enhancing this selectivity. Option 1 reports higher selectivity for NSeqs over RSeqs in naive females and enhanced selectivity after social experience, which supports the paper's central claim that predictive sequences matter and are plastically encoded. Option 2 reports the opposite, undermining that account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that seizures transiently depress the HCVR and cause hypothermia via impaired serotonergic function, with postictal 5-HT enhancement as a preventive strategy. Option 1 reports this depression (decreased HCVR, hypoventilation, hypothermia, and mortality worsened by PCPA, rescued by fenfluramine), which is consistent with and supports the proposed 5-HT-mediated mechanism and the biomarker/prevention rationale. Option 2 reverses the direction (increased HCVR, hyperventilation, hyperthermia), which would contradict the proposed serotonergic-depression account.

The paper proposes that early-life stress degrades temporal processing and that this degradation of sensory fidelity could contribute to cognitive problems. Option 1 reports impaired detection of long gaps with enhanced neural responses to gaps, which fits a story of miscoding and degraded representations (the paper's account of ELS-induced vulnerability). Option 2 reports impaired detection of short gaps with reduced neural responses, which is a more internally coherent degradation story in that reduced responses would plausibly explain reduced detection, but it still supports the same hypothesis of ELS degrading sensory fidelity. Both support the proposed account, but Option 1's mismatch of enhanced responses with impaired behavior is less clearly interpretable as degraded fidelity, so Option 2 is somewhat better news for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same framing: opioid receptors modulate PVT activity, with reduced modulation after morphine exposure via desensitization and internalization. The key difference is direction. Option 1 reports that opioid receptor activation enhances PVT firing and inhibitory transmission, while Option 2 reports suppression. Option 2 also says reduced modulation follows chronic rather than acute exposure. The paper's proposed account is that opioid receptors act on PVT and that receptor desensitization and internalization reduce modulation after morphine. Option 1's enhancement with acute-exposure desensitization is a coherent, specific mechanism; Option 2's suppression with chronic-exposure desensitization is equally coherent. Neither clearly favors the paper's account more, so the balance is near even, with a slight edge to Option 1 for the acute-exposure desensitization framing matching the proposed mechanism more directly.

The paper proposes that paired LAS-TMS induces plasticity, specifically an increase in corticoreticular connection efficacy, and promotes the protocol as a useful new tool. Option 1 reports LTP-like enhancement of TMS responses, which supports the proposed mechanism and the protocol's utility. Option 2 reports LTD-like depression, which would contradict the claimed potentiation of corticoreticular connections and weaken the proposed utility. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts are identical in framing and conclusions; they differ only in which SSRI is studied (escitalopram/fluoxetine vs sertraline/paroxetine) and the corresponding numbers, which are the same values assigned to different drugs. The paper's proposed account (compartmentalized SSRI-SERT interactions in membranes/organelles) is supported equally by both versions, so the difference is not good or bad news for the proposed account.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: sleep loss shifts brain morphology in an aging-like direction and is reversible by recovery sleep. The only difference is the magnitude of brain-age increase after total sleep deprivation: 1-2 years in Option 1 versus 4-5 years in Option 2. A larger aging-like shift provides stronger support for the paper's proposed account that sleep loss accelerates brain aging, so Option 2 is better news for the hypothesis. Option 1's smaller effect is weaker support, though still consistent with the account.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of vmPFC activation for positive versus negative feedback on highly dependent traits. Option 1 reports that positive feedback yields less vmPFC activation and negative feedback more, which fits the paper's proposed account of selectively attenuating threatening feedback to preserve positivity and coherence. Option 2 reverses this pattern, which would undercut the constrained-updating mechanism the paper defends. So Option 1 is better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes a nutrient-sensitive RL model. Option 1 reports that recent rewards influenced choices less when containing preferred nutrients and that monkeys discarded preferred nutrients despite higher reward probability; Option 2 reports the opposite pattern (stronger influence and choosing preferred nutrients despite lower probability). Option 2's findings are more consistent with nutrient-driven subjective value guiding choice, which is the paper's central claim, so Option 1 is weaker support for the proposed model.

Both versions present the same design and claim that the self-concept is conceptualized as self-importance and represented in a single region. They differ only in the region: ACC in Option 1 versus mPFC in Option 2. The paper's proposed account is that self-importance is the key representational dimension; the choice of region is a secondary detail. Neither option is clearly better news for the paper's central claim, since both support it equally, so the difference is near neutral.

The paper proposes that rehabilitation restores neurovascular coupling and that the superior frontal gyrus is a neuromodulation target, with restoration of executive control and compensation of frontoparietal integration. Option 1 reports reduced CBF-fALFF correlation and increased CBF/fALFF in the superior frontal gyrus (linked to motor gains) with decreased thalamic ratio, which fits a restoration-plus-compensation account. Option 2 reports the opposite direction: enhanced global coupling and decreased superior frontal ratio, which would undercut the proposed executive-control mechanism. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's account.

The paper proposes a multimodal MRI-LSM correlation platform and MRI signatures as biomarkers. Option 1 reports quantitative MRI differences between tumor and contralateral hemisphere and model-specific signatures that differ greatly, which supports the utility of MRI metrics as tumor biomarkers that can be decoded and used clinically. Option 2 reports no MRI differences and only slight signature differences, undermining the value of the MRI biomarkers the paper advocates. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed approach.

The two abstracts differ in whether VIP cells and the square-wave bursting mechanism are described as regular or irregular firing, and in naming the late-spiking cell type (Chandelier vs neurogliaform). The paper's proposed account is that VIP cells' firing arises from strong adaptation interacting with a slowly inactivating K+ channel, and that the bursting mechanism explains the firing pattern. Option 1's regular firing is the mechanistically coherent, explained pattern for adaptation-driven VIP firing; Option 2's irregular firing is a less natural fit for an adaptation-plus-slow-K+ explanation. So Option 1 supports the paper's account somewhat better.

The paper proposes that acidification suppresses seizures by reducing excitatory pyramidal neuron firing via NaV1.2 inhibition, with interneurons unaffected. Option 1 matches this mechanism exactly. Option 2 reverses it, claiming interneuron firing is reduced while pyramidal firing is unaffected, which would undermine the proposed account of seizure suppression through reduced excitation. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that C. elegans has multiple new inhibitory ligand-gated channels and a polymodal channel. Option 1 reports choline as the primary ligand for the inhibitory channels, a surprising and specific finding that strengthens the novelty of the ligand-receptor pairs. It also reports aminergic activation of LGC-39, which fits the polymodal claim. Option 2 reports acetylcholine as the primary ligand, which is less novel, and histamine instead of an aminergic ligand, which is a narrower claim. Option 1 therefore reads as stronger support for the proposed diverse repertoire.

The two abstracts differ only in whether EE's mitigating effect on RS decline is most pronounced when evidence accumulation rates are shallowest (Option 1) or steepest (Option 2). The paper proposes that EEG evidence accumulation metrics index neurocognitive vulnerability and that cognitive reserve operates in neurophysiological markers. Option 1 makes the reserve effect concentrated in the vulnerable (shallow-slope) group, which fits a story where EE buffers those with the weakest accumulation, supporting the vulnerability-indexing claim. Option 2 would place the benefit in efficient accumulators, which is less obviously a vulnerability story. So Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same framing: synaptic changes support memory, and the paper proposes synapse-specific, state-dependent modulation that may aid consolidation. Option 1 reports coherent, specific, interpretable patterns (wake-up at PP-DG, NREM-up at SC-CA1, REM-down at Fx-NAc, weak modulation at Fx-PFC/Fx-Amy) that fit a synapse-specific consolidation account. Option 2 has garbled, internally inconsistent statements (a bracketed fragment, REM increase at PP-DG/SC-CA1 contradicting the NREM framing, and strong modulation at Fx-PFC/Fx-Amy that conflicts with the correlation pattern), which weakens support for the proposed account. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

Both options share the same core claim that beta oscillations encode RPE in striatum. They differ only in which striatal territory dominates: Option 1 says dorsal (sensorimotor and associative) stronger than ventral, Option 2 says ventral stronger than dorsal. The paper's proposed account emphasizes beta-band RPE encoding and a contribution of a specific striatal division. Option 1 supports a dorsal-striatum account of learning updates, which aligns with the paper's framing of dorsal contribution as a major finding; Option 2 would undercut that emphasis. Hence Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that chronic ethanol tolerance is a distinct memory-like state molecularly separate from rapid tolerance. Option 1 states chronic tolerance is independent of Hr38/Nr4a and suppressed by Sirt1, while rapid tolerance is enhanced by Sirt1, reinforcing the molecular distinction between forms. Option 2 instead makes chronic tolerance Hr38-dependent and enhanced by Sirt1, which would blur the claimed molecular separation between chronic and rapid tolerance. Option 1 therefore better supports the paper's central account of distinct molecular bases.

The two abstracts differ only in the causal ordering of PKCδ relative to TrkB and DAG. Option 1 says PKCδ activation leads to TrkB and DAG production, placing PKCδ upstream. Option 2 says PKCδ is activated downstream of TrkB and DAG, which fits the canonical signaling model and the paper's dual-role framing. The paper's proposed account is that PKCδ is a facilitator of plasticity acting on both local spine and nuclear transcription; the upstream-of-TrkB/DAG claim in Option 1 is a less standard and less mechanistically coherent position, so Option 2 is somewhat better news for the proposed account.

The paper proposes that aberrant astrocyte signaling (elevated Ca2+/NFAT4 activation, larger individual transients) drives cerebrovascular and synaptic dysfunction in HHcy, and that inhibiting NFAT via VIVIT is therapeutic. Option 1 reports larger individual astrocyte Ca2+ transients and increased NFAT4 activation under HHcy, which supports the aberrant-signaling account. Option 2 reports smaller transients and decreased NFAT4 activation, which would undercut the proposed mechanism. Option 1 is therefore much better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in the oscillation band named for the brain states: theta (Option 1) versus gamma (Option 2). The paper's proposed account is that information storage and sharing are disrupted in epilepsy, shifting toward disorder, with brain-state selectivity lost. Whether theta or gamma states are the stereotypic states does not change the direction of that finding, so neither option is clearly better news for the proposed mechanism. Option 1 is marginally more conventional for hippocampal-entorhinal state organization, but that is a weak difference.

The paper proposes that ensembles form via experience-dependent changes and maintain distinct identity through differential firing and decorrelation. Option 1 reports decorrelation, decoupling, decreased excitability and connectivity, which supports ensemble segregation and identity preservation as framed by the paper's account. Option 2 reports coupling and increased correlation, which undercuts the claim that ensembles are functionally distinct and decorrelated. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The two abstracts are identical except for the specific neural networks named in the spatiotemporal progression. Option 1 names posterior temporal, frontoparietal, inferior parietal, and salience network nodes; Option 2 names hippocampal/anterior temporal, frontotemporal, inferior frontal, and default mode network nodes. The paper's proposed model is the temporally specified cascade of semantic processing networks. Option 1's account is the more internally coherent with the stated network-level claims about semantic retrieval and syntactic reappraisal, though neither version is clearly better supported by the methods described. The difference is modest, so the probability sits moderately above even.

Both abstracts propose the same hypothesis: continuity of opioid administration is protective, and interruption enhances subsequent responses. Option 1 reports that continuous morphine elevates D2-MSN output (canonically pro-reward), with interruption not dampening it as much, which fits the paper's hypothesis that interruption enhances abuse-related responses, i.e., continuity is protective. Option 2 instead reports dampened D1-MSN output under continuous morphine, which is a less direct fit with the reward-promoting framing the authors invoke. Option 1's finding is more coherent with the proposed account, so it is somewhat better news for it. The shift in region (core vs shell) matters little to this judgment.

The paper proposes a shared-yet-linked population coding scheme in which risky and safe options overlap in neural code (correlated, collinear subspaces) yet are linked by a linear transform enabling comparison. Option 1 reports detectable overlap and similar subspaces, which supports this proposed multiplexed account of comparison across dissimilar option types. Option 2 reports no overlap and distinct subspaces, which undercuts the shared-code, linear-transform comparison mechanism the paper defends. So Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

Both abstracts propose the same account: a ramping/sustained dopamine signal, distinct from phasic RPE, reflecting anticipation or incentivization of action. Option 1 reports a ramp that is affected by probabilistic reward, increases with shorter cues, and grows when timing is less predictable, which fits the proposed account of the ramp depending on and modulating the RPE signal. Option 2 reports the ramp as unaffected by probabilistic reward and as a plateau scaling with longer cues, which weakens the claim that the ramp is tied to the RPE-based account. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed account better.

Both abstracts share the same framing and proposed account: that binge drinkers show blunted motivational encoding for non-alcohol stimuli, supporting the ERV-based aberrant learning model. Option 1 reports that results support the hypotheses, the blunted ERV signal, and the correlation with problematic use, which strengthens the paper's proposed account. Option 2 reports results refuting the hypotheses, which weakens the account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed hypothesis.

The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 reports black responses dominating and black stimuli producing stronger suppression, while Option 2 reports white responses dominating and white stimuli producing stronger suppression. The paper proposes feedforward and recurrent mechanisms with delayed, polarity-selective cortical suppression explaining the asymmetry. Option 1 is therefore a finding consistent with the paper's account of asymmetry, but the direction of polarity is the only difference, so neither is clearly better news for the proposed mechanism. Overall the difference is essentially neutral with respect to the hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in the brain region named: Option 1 says the prior threat trace was expected only in the right amygdala and found widespread in the amygdala, while Option 2 names the right hippocampus. The paper's proposed account is that verbal instructions do not fully override experience-based CS representations, which lingers more widely than the Pavlovian-trace literature predicted. Option 1 frames the finding as confirming the amygdala as the locus of the trace, which fits a classic associative-learning account that the paper engages with; Option 2 shifts the locus to the hippocampus, which is less central to the amygdala-based fear circuitry the paper is testing. Both support the main claim equally, so the difference is modest, leaning slightly toward Option 1 as more coherent with the stated expectations.

The paper proposes that EM tomography gives the most accurate description of the rod synapse and that detachment-induced changes disrupt rod-pathway signaling. Option 1 reports the hilus contracting, obscuring the sequestered invagination environment; Option 2 reports it enlarging, exposing that environment. Both are hypothetical. Option 2's enlargement and exposure is the more naturally disruptive account, consistent with the paper's claim that changes disrupt information flow, whereas contraction is a less direct route to disruption. So Option 1 is weaker news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that conversational turn-taking indexes prosocial interaction. Option 1 reports reduced turn-taking in virtual settings, which would suggest virtual interaction impairs prosocial exchange, a finding the paper's framing treats as concerning and motivating design improvements. Option 2 reports increased turn-taking virtually, which would be read as virtual interaction being more prosocial by the paper's own metric, a more favorable result for its turn-taking account. Thus Option 2 is better news for the proposed measure, making Option 1 less favorable.

The paper's central claim is that dlPFC physiology follows a smooth gradient spanning regions rather than discrete areal boundaries. Option 1 reports a smooth gradient and says it invalidates functional boundaries between anatomical regions, which supports the paper's proposed account. Option 2 reports an areal gradient, which would undercut the paper's framing. Both keep the distributed-representation finding, so the difference lies in the gradient-type conclusion, which Option 1 supports.

The paper proposes that dopamine agonist therapy potentiates risk-taking via cue-amplified dopaminergic signaling and frontostriatal decoupling. Option 1 reports ropinirole increasing risky choice, increased win-stay, suppressed midbrain activity, and decoupling that perpetuates risk, all supporting the proposed account. Option 2 reports the opposite direction for each finding (decreased risk, enhanced midbrain activity, coupling that reduces risk), which contradicts the hypothesis that dopamine agonists promote risk-taking. Option 1 is therefore much better news for the paper's proposed mechanism.

The paper argues that context matters and that studies using little-context stimuli may not generalize to natural language. Option 1 reports more context lowering SNR and semantic representation, which undercuts the case for natural-language stimuli as a better window into meaning and weakens the paper's generalization argument. Option 2 reports context raising SNR and semantic representation, strongly supporting the paper's call for natural-language paradigms. Option 2 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that peroxynitrite drives migraine-related nociceptive sensitization and that targeting PN is therapeutically promising. Option 2 shows PN neutralization attenuating hypersensitivity, priming, 3-NT increases, and neuronal hyperexcitability, which supports that account. Option 1 shows the opposite: PN neutralization enhances these responses, which would undercut the proposed PN-driven mechanism and its therapeutic angle. Option 2 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper's proposed account is that PCB exposure during development sensitizes the auditory system to later noise, producing failed recovery, tonotopic disruption, and damage linked to oxidative stress. Option 1 reports increased GABAergic inhibition, which is consistent with a maladaptive synaptic reorganization story but framed as the mechanism of damage. Option 2 reports reduced inhibition, which would weaken the paper's account of inhibition-driven dysfunction. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed mechanism somewhat better, though the direction of inhibition change is only one component of the overall account.

The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 reports increases in AMPAR conductance or nonconductive properties as the expression mechanism of E2-induced potentiation, while Option 2 reports decreases. Potentiation is by definition an enhancement of synaptic strength, so an increase in AMPAR conductance or nonconductive properties is consistent with the paper's proposed account of E2-induced potentiation. Option 2 would contradict the potentiation the paper defends, so Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed mechanism.

The paper proposes that the basal forebrain and DAN drive the hippocampus toward external and internal attention. Option 2 reports the predicted pattern: stronger BF-hippocampus connectivity during external-heavy task, stronger DAN-hippocampus connectivity during internal task, and a brain-behavior correlation in the memory-guided task, supporting the hypothesis. Option 1 reports the opposite directions and a null/contrary brain-behavior result, undermining the hypothesis and suggesting these networks may not modulate the hippocampus this way. Option 2 is clearly better news for the proposed account.

Both options are identical except Option 1 reports contralateral lateral pRN targeting while Option 2 reports ipsilateral medial pRN targeting. The paper's proposed account is that the corticorubral pathway is somatotopically organized and that the RN reduces cortical influence after injury; Option 1's contralateral, anatomically expected projection pattern (corticorubral fibers cross and target the contralateral RN) is more consistent with the established pathway and the paper's framing, so it is modestly better news for its account. The difference is a topographic detail rather than a core result, so the effect is moderate.

The paper proposes that GVS is encoded with nonlinear, asymmetric dynamics that produce a directional bias in central integration, challenging current models. Option 1 reports exactly this nonlinear, asymmetric finding, which supports the paper's core claim and mechanistic account. Option 2 reports linear, symmetric responses, which would undercut the proposed account and the stated explanation of directional bias. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that CDKL5 kinase activity is required for presynaptic synaptic vesicle recycling in CDD. Option 1 (endocytosis) and Option 2 (exocytosis) differ only in which step is affected. Both support the same kinase-dependent presynaptic role. The claimed mechanism is the same either way; the step differs. Endocytosis is the step the paper's framing emphasizes as its central finding, and the abstract's logic (selective requirement, rescue by kinase domain) is equally coherent for both. Relative to the proposed account, neither option is clearly better news, though Option 1 matches the title-level framing slightly more.

The paper's framing (overactivations reflect neuronal origin, supporting a neural-resource/compensation view) is strengthened in Option 1, where BOLD overactivations are coupled with increased glucose metabolism, indicating synaptic activity. Option 2 instead concludes overactivations are non-neuronal, undermining the neuronal/compensatory account the paper defends. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of olfactory bulb neurogenesis change in α-syn-Tg mice: increased (Option 1) versus reduced (Option 2). The paper's proposed account is that neurogenesis alterations contribute to olfactory dysfunction in PD-like mice. Reduced neurogenesis would be a plausible contributor to deficits and fits a neurodegeneration-style narrative, while increased neurogenesis is more ambiguous as a mechanism but could still contribute to dysfunction via aberrant integration. Given the paper frames both changes as potential contributors, the difference is modestly favorable to Option 2 as supporting its account of a neurogenesis-linked deficit mechanism, though not decisively.

The paper proposes that reduced Hrs/ESCRT-0 impairs ubiquitinated protein clearance, causing synaptic deregulation and accelerated neurodegeneration. Option 1 states accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and increased surface PrPC, consistent with the proposed mechanism of hampered clearance and neurotoxic signaling. Option 2 reports reduced ubiquitinated proteins and decreased PrPC with the conclusion that Hrs reduction promotes clearance, which contradicts the paper's proposed account of impaired clearance driving disease. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's hypothesis far better.

The paper proposes that immature cortical astrocytes integrate, mature, and retain cortical identity after transplantation, including in the cerebellum. Option 1 reports that transplanted astrocytes in cerebellum retain cortical features via lower GLT1, higher GLAST, and increased GluA1, which shows intrinsic identity persisting in a foreign region, supporting the cell-autonomous account. Option 2 reports higher GLT1, lower GLAST, and no GluA1, which would suggest more environmental adaptation toward cerebellar identity and weaker support for retained cortical properties. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's central claim.

Both abstracts share the same core claims: vestibular contribution to neck muscle control across dynamic range, absence after vestibular loss, and no visual influence. They differ in two findings. Option 1 reports low-frequency responses enhanced under concurrent broadband motion and vestibular responses diminished by arousal; Option 2 reports attenuation and enhancement respectively. The paper's proposed account is that vestibular input is integrated with other inputs for postural control; Option 1's enhancement of low-frequency responses via multi-frequency context and arousal-driven suppression is less consistent with a clean integrative account of rich vestibular feedback, while Option 2's reported modulations align more with an active, arousal-boosted vestibular contribution. Overall, Option 2 is somewhat better news for the paper's framing.

The paper's framing centers on gain-of-function variants causing hyperexcitability disorders, and it argues the mechanism is cell-type specific. Option 1 reports hyperexcitability in L2/3 pyramidal neurons, consistent with the expected disease mechanism (GOF leads to hyperexcitability), while Option 2 reverses this, showing hypoexcitability in L2/3, which would undercut the proposed account of how these variants impair forebrain function. Both options share the same CA1 directionality difference relative to L2/3 pattern, so the key difference lies in L2/3 results, which favor Option 1 as better support for the paper's defended hypothesis.

Both abstracts describe the same design and hypothesis; they differ only in the transmitter studied (glutamate vs GABA). The paper's proposed account is that AIS-targeting inputs provide an inhibitory 'veto' on action potential initiation across developmental polarity changes. Option 1 (glutamate) reports inhibition of AP initiation via NMDA shunts, which is a surprising, novel finding that fits the paper's framing as a notable mechanism. Option 2 (GABA) reports the same inhibitory veto via GABAA shunts, which is the more conventionally expected result and matches the classic shunting-inhibition account. The paper's proposed veto account is supported equally by both, but the glutamate version is more striking news for a non-canonical mechanism the paper defends, so Option 1 is modestly better news.

The two abstracts differ in direction: Option 1 reports release rising with higher firing frequency and spike number, and Ca2+ currents increasing after orchidectomy, which supports the paper's conclusion that gonadal feedback removal enhances stimulus-secretion coupling. Option 2 reverses these directions (release rising with lower firing, decreasing spike number, decreasing Ca2+ currents), which contradicts the paper's proposed account of firing-release coupling and its enhanced-efficacy conclusion. Option 1 is therefore much better news for the paper's defended account.

The paper proposes that Syt11 inhibits EndoA1-mediated SV endocytosis, supported by Syt11 deficiency accelerating endocytosis and the peptide inhibiting endocytosis in wild-type but not EndoA1-knockdown neurons. Option 1 states Syt11 inhibits EndoA1 and the peptide blocks endocytosis, consistent with the proposed model. Option 2 reverses this, stating Syt11 facilitates EndoA1 and the peptide enhances endocytosis, which contradicts the paper's central inhibitory mechanism. Option 1 is clearly better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The two abstracts are identical except for the neurotransmitter (GABA vs glutamate) and which Cav subtype (Cav2.3 vs Cav2.2) boosts vesicle recruitment during sustained high-frequency transmission. The paper's proposed account is that Cav2.3 is specifically required to sustain transmission during prolonged activity, which Option 1 reports. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's central claim, while Option 2 reports the opposite subtype. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that suppressing inflammation with minocycline preserves Ia-motoneuron synapses and that this preservation is necessary and sufficient to restore synaptic and reflex function. Option 1 reports that preservation is necessary for overcoming functional decline, that minocycline has a general capacity to rescue sensorimotor behavior, and that structural preservation ensures normal function, all supporting the hypothesis. Option 2 says preservation is not sufficient and that minocycline has only limited capacity, which undercuts the paper's account.

The paper proposes that rTMS acts through microglial cytokine release (TNFα, IL6) to promote plasticity. Option 1 reports that cytokine substitution preserves plasticity without microglia and that microglia depletion abolishes rTMS effects, supporting the microglia-cytokine-plasticity account. Option 2 reports the opposite: cytokine substitution reduces plasticity, depletion increases rTMS effects, and the conclusion is suppression of cytokine release. Option 2 contradicts the paper's proposed mechanism, so Option 1 is clearly better news for it.

The paper argues that aberrant (increased) macrophage activation in the stria vascularis drives age-related strial dysfunction and hearing loss. Option 1 reports increased macrophage activation with age tied to declining hearing, which supports the paper's proposed mechanism. Option 2 reports decreased activation, which would contradict the proposed macrophage-driven account. So Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that CDC25B and G2 phase length control the balance between direct and indirect neurogenesis. Option 1 reports a G2 lengthening with a shift toward TBR1+ neurons and away from TBR2+ basal progenitors, with the defect tied to G2 length and CDK1 interaction, which directly supports the proposed mechanism. Option 2 swaps the markers (TBR2 neurons, TBR1 progenitors, which are mislabeled) and attributes the effect to G1 lengthening, contradicting the paper's G2-centered account. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper's proposed account is that VLC-FA loss in the ELOVL4 mutant causes synaptic dysfunction in SCA34. Option 1 reports the findings the paper's framing most naturally supports: reduced excitatory mEPSC frequency (presynaptic defect), enhanced inhibitory transmission, reduced PF-PC paired-pulse ratio, larger RRP, and reduced spine density, which fit a consistent pathological picture of impaired cerebellar synapses. Option 2 reverses these, pointing to a different and less clearly coherent mechanism, so Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that Axin1 uniquely regulates cortical dendritic arborization via a γC3-dependent mechanism through the VCD. Option 1 frames Axin1 as the upstream factor acting through γC3, matching the paper's central proposed mechanism (Axin1 knockout disrupts γC3 localization and dendritic complexity; rescue shows Axin1 acts via γC3 VCD). Option 2 reverses the direction, making γC3 the upstream factor acting through Axin1, which is a different and weaker account of the mechanism the paper defends. Option 1 therefore supports the proposed hypothesis more directly.

The paper's core claim is that ganglion cells encode combinations of presaccadic and postsaccadic images, with signal processing beyond simple light steps, and that On/Off asymmetries exist. Option 1 attributes the image-change sensitivity and beyond-step-response processing to On parasol and Large On cells, with Off cells explained by simple step responses. Option 2 reverses this, attributing those to Off parasol and Large Off cells. Both support the same general account; the difference is only which polarity carries the extra interactions. Option 1 fits the paper's framing of distinct response patterns and asymmetries equally well, so the news value for the proposed account is roughly neutral with a slight edge depending on which polarity is considered the more striking finding.

Both abstracts propose the same hypothesis: PVT MC3R neurons link energy status to anxiety circuitry. Option 1 reports activation by aversive stimuli, anxiogenic effects of activation, feeding suppression, and anxiolytic effects of inhibition, which coherently supports the proposed pathway as an anxiety-promoting, appetite-suppressing node. Option 2 reverses all these directions, yielding an anxiolytic, appetite-promoting node, which is inconsistent with the framing around aversive and anorexigenic signals. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed account more strongly.

The two abstracts differ only in whether spindles shift abruptly (Option 1) or gradually (Option 2) with age, and in whether reversal is stronger at higher or lower slow-wave frequency. The paper's proposed account emphasizes a gradual change starting at midlife that opens a window for early intervention. A gradual, progressive shift fits that framing better than an abrupt one, so Option 2 is somewhat better news for the paper's account. The frequency direction difference is less clearly favorable either way.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of total brain size change in humans: Option 1 says XXY increases and XYY decreases brain size; Option 2 says XXY decreases and XYY increases it. The paper's framework and conclusions emphasize cross-species comparison and conserved regional effects, with the human-specific global effect as a finding. Option 1 is the more plausible/consistent with prior reports of XXY (Klinefelter) associated with reduced brain volume and XYY with increased, so Option 2 is the more expected direction, making Option 1 somewhat worse news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ in which LPB projection responds to heat versus cold and which mediates heat versus cold avoidance. Option 1 has LPB→MnPO neurons carrying heat signals and mediating heat avoidance, with LPB→CeA mediating cold avoidance and cold-activated; this matches a clean division of labor between thermoregulatory (MnPO) and emotional (CeA) pathways that the paper's framework emphasizes. Option 2 swaps these roles, which would be less parsimonious with the proposed segregated framework. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed account better.

The paper proposes that normal PrRP signaling protects against stress disorders. Option 1 reports PrRP hyperpolarizing MCH neurons ex vivo, REM-active MCH cell suppression, PrRP overactivation in stress, and increased passive coping, which mainly supports a model where PrRP drives inhibition and maladaptive stress responses. Option 2 reports depolarization, NREM-active cell increase, deactivation of PrRP cells, and decreased active coping, framing PrRP as protective and more active. Option 2 aligns more with a protective PrRP account, so Option 1 is worse news for the proposed hypothesis.

Both abstracts describe the same method and hypothesis of layer-specific entorhinal activation. The difference is the condition mapping: Option 1 reports superficial layers tied to resting-state encoding and deep layers to consolidation, which fits the paper's proposed account of separate encoding and consolidation pathways. Option 2 reports superficial and deep layers tied to task-related encoding and retrieval, a more conventional and less specific mapping. The paper's defended account of dissociable layer-specific encoding/consolidation processing is more directly supported by Option 1's result, so it is somewhat better news, though both are positive.

The paper defends the view that DNNs fail to fully capture higher-level ventral-stream dynamics and that visuo-semantic, nameable features explain unexplained variance. Option 1 has DNNs explaining early lower-level areas (66 ms) and visuo-semantic features taking over later in higher-level areas (146 ms), a temporally plausible gradual reversal that supports the paper's account. Option 2 swaps the timings so visuo-semantic features explain higher-level dynamics from 66 ms and DNNs only lower areas from 146 ms, which is less coherent with a feedforward hierarchy and weakens the proposed gradual reversal. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's proposal.

The two abstracts differ in whether motor and tactile finger representations overlap (Option 1) or are distinct (Option 2), and in which modality is best described by finger kinematics in the polydactyly case. The paper's central proposal is that sensorimotor finger representations converge toward a perceived hand model. Option 1's overlapping representations, integrating motor and tactile information, fit an integrated sensorimotor account more naturally than Option 2's distinct representations. Option 1 also keeps the perceived model dominant for motor representations, which is consistent with the convergence claim. Option 2 instead has kinematics explaining motor representations, slightly weakening the perceived-model story. Overall Option 1 is modestly better news for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same design and first and third results; they differ only in whether unexpected or expected material behaviors show stronger decoding within 190 ms. The paper's proposed account is that expectation violations trigger additional processing demands, which Option 1 reports (unexpected decoded better) and Option 2 reverses (expected decoded better, framed as meeting expectations requiring processing). Option 1 thus better supports the paper's violation-of-expectation account, so it is better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper's proposed account is that dark-dominance stems from slower inhibition to dark stimuli, and it is supported by dark-dominance appearing only in early latencies. Option 1 (early-only dark-dominance, less orientation selectivity in dark-dominated neurons) fits this timing-based account and the link to faster responses, so it reads as better support. Option 2 (dark-dominance also in late latencies, more orientation selectivity) weakens the early-latency explanation and the proposed mechanism.

Option 1 reports that macaques show similar, human-like exploitation of goal redundancy: greater variability for the wide goal, ignoring jumps for the wide goal, and matching latencies. This supports the paper's defended account that monkeys can serve as a model for optimal feedback control. Option 2 reports increased ability, reduced variability, following rather than ignoring the jump, and differing from humans, which undermines the claim that monkeys model human redundancy exploitation. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that proactive attentional mechanisms support predictive distractor processing, with early visual cortex excitability tracking distractor probability. Option 1 reports increased excitability at high-probability distractor locations, framed as predictive distractor selection. Option 2 reports reduced excitability there, framed as predictive distractor suppression. Since the behavioral literature cited shows expected distractors become less interfering, suppression fits the proposed account better. Option 2 is therefore the better news for the paper's hypothesis, so Option 1 is less favorable.

Both versions propose GPR173 as a novel CCK receptor mediating cortical CCK interneuron signaling. Option 1 claims CCK knockout abolishes inhibitory LTP and proposes GPR173 as CCK3R mediating inhibitory LTP, which directly supports the paper's account of GPR173 as a therapeutic target for E/I imbalance. Option 2 has inconsistencies (HFLS knock-out, excitatory LTP, CCK1R) that weaken the proposed mechanism and do not clearly tie GPR173 to the inhibitory synapse enhancement the paper centers on. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's account.

The paper proposes two dissociable scene systems (categorization vs. visually guided navigation). Option 1 reports navigation developing earlier than categorization and WS adults impaired in categorization but spared in navigation, which is the pattern predicting dissociation with the specific timelines and breakdown the authors argue for. Option 2 reverses both findings, yielding a different dissociation pattern that still shows dissociation but with the opposite ordering. The hypothesis of dissociable systems is supported in both, but Option 1 matches the paper's framing of action-sparing/perception-impaired expectations less neatly than one might expect; still, Option 1 more directly fits the prior notion of WS sparing perception-based scene categorization relative to navigation only in the reverse sense. Given the authors' emphasis, the Option 1 pattern is modestly better news for their account.

The paper proposes that VP GABA neurons encode reward expectation and that their calcium activity encodes cue-elicited reward-seeking vigor. Option 1 reports cue-evoked excitation, behavior-suppressing inhibition during cues, and reward-time excitation, all of which fit a model where VP GABA activity drives and tracks reward seeking. Option 2 reports the opposite signs (cue inhibition, excitation suppressing seeking, reward-time inhibition), which undermines the proposed encoding account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that cortical areas with insufficient interictal activity are seizure-vulnerable and that global scaling of cortical activity above healthy levels is protective. Option 1 reports decreased overlap of interictal events with the emergence zone and higher global intensity predicting lower seizure burden, which supports the paper's account. Option 2 reports the opposite direction (excessive activity, scaling below healthy levels), which contradicts the proposed mechanism of protection via elevated activity. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in whether astrocyte activity is depressed (Option 1) or elevated (Option 2) relative to unshocked controls across days and extinction. The paper's proposed account is that amygdalar astrocytes are real-time participants in fear processing and respond to fear-associated context. Persistent elevation after shock in Option 2 would more directly support an active, sustained astrocytic role in fear memory, whereas depression in Option 1 is a less intuitive but still meaningful signal of involvement. Option 2 therefore reads as somewhat better news for the paper's account, so Option 1 is slightly less favorable.

The paper's proposed method is the nanoGFP nanoprobe approach. Option 1 reports slower lateral diffusion with nanoprobes (decreased D), while Option 2 reports faster diffusion (increased D). The paper's central message is that nanoprobes are a better, less perturbing tool, and that the antiGFP-QD605 IgG probe is a more reliable reference. Slower diffusion from nanoprobes would suggest the probes cross-link or hinder receptor mobility, which undermines the claim that nanoprobes measure native behavior; faster diffusion would be the less concerning direction for a probe-validation claim framed around minimal perturbation. Thus Option 1 is worse news for the proposed method, so the probability favors Option 2.

Both abstracts claim individual neurons can be driven with excitation or inhibition via stimulation site choice, supporting the paper's proposed approach of direct single-neuron control. The only difference is the spatial pattern: Option 1 says inhibition is local and excitation distributed; Option 2 reverses this. Which pattern is 'better news' for the paper's control approach is ambiguous, since both still show bidirectional control; the difference is a spatial detail rather than a clear gain or loss for the proposed method. Slight lean toward Option 1 as its local-inhibition/distributed-excitation account is the more conventional framing of microstimulation, but the difference is minor.

The two versions differ only in the direction of GMD change mediating the age-related increase in positive feedback learning: Option 1 reports reduced GMD, Option 2 reports elevated GMD. The paper frames brain maturation as yielding more efficient organization, and it putatively links this to lower GMD (Option 1 explicitly says 'putatively reflected in lower GMD' and 'reduced GMD'). Option 1 thus matches the paper's maturation-efficiency account, which the paper defends, so it is better news for that account.

The paper proposes that IL activity and its outputs (IL-NAshell, IL-amygdala) are needed to encode extinction contingencies. Option 1 reports that inhibiting these pathways right after unreinforced presses impairs extinction retention and increases lever pressing, which supports the proposed network's role in encoding extinction. Option 2 reports the opposite: inhibition enhances retention and decreases pressing, which would argue against a required encoding role for these pathways. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same framework and behavioral findings. The key difference is Option 1 reports the cue modulates α frequency in a retinotopic manner and ipsilateral synchronization/contralateral desynchronization coding confidence, which matches the paper's proposed account that α frequency (sampling) drives perceptual accuracy and α amplitude drives metacognition. Option 2 instead reports γ frequency modulation and reversed lateralization, which weakens the α-frequency sampling account the paper defends. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed mechanism better.

The paper proposes that dCA1 neuronal activity changes, specifically the response dynamics of individual neurons and ensembles, underlie contextual memory retrieval. Option 1 reports decreased responses in conditioned context, specific to that context, scaling with memory strength, and tied to SWR events. Option 2 reports increased responses with the same specificity and scaling. The paper's framing of a 'portion of neurons increasing responses' with decreased population response is contrasted; the hypothesis that neuronal response changes encode memory recall is supported in both, but Option 2's increase is the more straightforward engram-style account of memory being represented by enhanced activity of recruited neurons, which aligns more cleanly with the paper's proposed mechanism of specific, strength-proportional activation. Option 1 is somewhat weaker support for a clean mechanistic account, so Option 2 is modestly better news for the paper's proposal.

The paper proposes that cholinergic regulation of BLa afferents is complex and pathway-specific. Option 1 attributes the biphasic phasic-ACh effect and the strong muscarinic suppression to the cortical (prelimbic) input, with thalamic input showing weaker suppression and a distinct mechanism. Option 2 swaps which pathway carries these properties. Both versions support the same overall thesis of pathway specificity; the difference is only which input is the main site, so the net news for the paper's claim is essentially neutral.

The paper proposes that P2X7R regulates dendritic outgrowth differently under physiological and pathological conditions, and that its activation under MIA drives schizophrenia-like deficits. Option 1 reports branching deficits and MIA-induced deficits in WT but not KO neurons, which supports the paper's account that P2X7R activation under pathology causes harmful dendritic changes linked to schizophrenia-like phenotypes. Option 2 reports surpluses, which would not fit the deficit-based schizophrenia link the paper draws. So Option 1 is better news for the proposed account.

The two abstracts differ only in the anatomical node reported: Option 1 names dorsal striatum and substantia nigra, Option 2 names ventral striatum and VTA. The paper's proposed account is that losartan modulates midbrain-striato-frontal circuits and that the RAS is a treatment target. Option 2's ventral striatum and VTA fit the classic mesolimbic reward circuitry, which is more consistent with the paper's reward-salience framing and the DA-RAS interaction hypothesis from animal models. Option 1's dorsal striatum and SN findings are more associated with motor/habit circuitry, a less coherent fit with the social reward account, so Option 1 is somewhat weaker news for the proposed account.

The paper proposes that domain organization extends to subcortical pulvinar and that this is an overarching principle. Option 1 reports right lateralization for tools and a left amygdala shortcut for animals; Option 2 reports left lateralization for tools and right amygdala for animals.
